strengths: First training-free framework explicitly designed and tailored for concept unlearning in text-to-video diffusion models.

The introduction of contrastive PCA (cPCA) to refine the refusal vector is a clever and mathematically sound way to isolate the target concept while minimizing collateral damage to unrelated semantics.
Extremely efficient and practical: requires only 5 safe/unsafe multi-modal pairs and results in a closed-form weight update that adds zero inference-time latency or memory overhead.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple hazardous categories (pornography, gore, copyrights, public figures, and sequential action risks) utilizing recognized metrics (T2VSafetyBench, FVD, MM-Notox) and GPT-4 evaluations.
Excellent qualitative results (especially in the extensive appendix) demonstrating clean and context-preserving semantic removal.
weaknesses: Lack of direct comparisons with adapted text-to-image unlearning baselines (e.g., UCE, RECE) or fine-tuning approaches. Even if those methods are not natively designed for video, adapting them or comparing against a basic fine-tuning baseline would better contextualize the quantitative performance.

Limited exploration of generalization to other text-to-video architectures. The paper focuses primarily on Open-Sora. It would be valuable to discuss how the layer selection heuristic (updating the last three double blocks) translates to other architectures like CogVideo or HunyuanVideo.
The method currently only addresses unlearning one concept at a time. Sequential or joint unlearning of multiple concepts is listed as a limitation but not explored or evaluated.

The sensitivity of the refusal vector to the choice of the 5 curated safe/unsafe pairs is not thoroughly analyzed. An ablation study showing the impact of varying the prompt pairs would strengthen the robustness claims.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and critical topic: safety steering and concept unlearning in large-scale text-to-video (T2V) diffusion/transformer models.
Proposes a training-free, closed-form weight update method that requires no retraining or access to the full training dataset, adding zero inference-time computational overhead.
The integration of contrastive PCA (cPCA) to isolate the target 'unsafe' concept from the 'retain' set is a elegant way to minimize collateral damage to unrelated semantics.
Provides a thorough mathematical derivation of how the subspace-aware projection can be folded directly into the linear layer weights (FFN matrices).

Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluation using established metrics (T2VSafetyBench, FVD, MM-Notox) across multiple diverse risk categories (copyrights, pornography, action risks, gore, public figures).
weaknesses: A major limitation is the lack of comparison with existing concept erasure baselines. Although designed for image models, competitive baselines like Unified Concept Editing (UCE) or Reliable and Efficient Concept Erasure (RECE) could be adapted to the video model's cross-attention/FFN layers to demonstrate the relative superiority of the proposed cPCA-based approach.

The method requires multimodal pairs (both text prompts and images) for concept extraction, but the text is ambiguous about how the image inputs ($u_i^{img}$ and $s_i^{img}$) are obtained. Are they manually curated web images, or generated by the model itself prior to unlearning? This detail is crucial for reproducibility.

While the concept occurrence rate drops significantly (e.g., from 73% to 33% for Copyright and Trademarks, and 44.7% to 13.4% for Pornography), the remaining unsafe generation rate is still non-trivial. The paper lacks discussion on how to achieve complete suppression without corrupting generation quality.

The choice of target layers (double blocks 17–19 in Open-Sora) and hyperparameters (cPCA rank $k=100$) appears heuristic and highly specific to the Open-Sora architecture. It is unclear how easily these hyperparameters translate to other popular text-to-video architectures (e.g., CogVideoX or HunyuanVideo).
Figure 3 is of low visual quality; the axis labels, legends, and numbers are extremely small and illegible.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and timely problem: targeted concept removal (unlearning) in generative video diffusion models (e.g., Open-Sora) to prevent the generation of harmful, copyrighted, or inappropriate content.
The proposed method is training-free and computationally efficient, executing a closed-form weight edit on the feed-forward network (FFN) layers immediately following cross-attention blocks.
The paper includes a detailed mathematical derivation showing how the low-rank projection is absorbed into the weight matrices.

The qualitative results in the appendix across several categories (nudity, gore, copyright logos, dangerous actions, and public figures) are extensive and demonstrate clear visual changes aligning with the safety objectives.
weaknesses: Lack of baselines: The paper does not compare the proposed method with any other concept erasure or unlearning baseline. Even if prior methods like UCE or RECE were designed for text-to-image models, they can be adapted as baselines by applying them to the spatial/cross-attention layers of the Video Transformer. Alternatively, standard fine-tuning or LoRA-based unlearning baselines should be included to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed low-rank refusal vector approach.

Missing details on handling temporal/spatial dimensions: Video latent representations possess temporal (T), spatial (S), and channel (C) dimensions. Section 3 represents latent activations as simple vectors $x \in \mathbb{R}^H$. The authors do not explain how the temporal and spatial dimensions of the video latents are processed (e.g., averaged, flattened, or treated as independent token samples) to construct the covariance matrices $C_r$ and $C_e$. Since this is positioned as the first video-specific unlearning technique, clarifying how the temporal dimension is handled is crucial.

Evaluation completeness and residual safety leaks: Table 1 shows that even after censoring, certain categories still exhibit a high rate of unsafe content generation (e.g., Copyright and Trademarks remains at 33.0% and Pornography at 13.4%). Additionally, the paper mentions robustness against adversarial bypass but lacks quantitative evaluations under adversarial or 'jailbreak' prompts (e.g., using character substitutions or synonym-based evasion).

Clarity issues in figures and text: Figure 3 (both left and right subplots) and Figure 4 are extremely small, making the axis labels and details illegible. In Section 3.2 (page 5, Contrastive PCA paragraph), the text mentions 'Then similar to P, we can first center...'; however, 'P' is not defined in the text (it is likely a typo for 'R' or 'C_r').

strengths: Timely and highly relevant topic, addressing safety and concept unlearning in large-scale text-to-video generative models.

Methodological novelty: Successfully adapts activation-level steering (refusal vectors) into a training-free, closed-form weight update using contrastive PCA (cPCA) specifically designed for video diffusion models.

Excellent computational and data efficiency: The proposed method requires only 5 paired safe/unsafe prompts and negligible compute (~0.4 GPU hours, ~1$ cost) to sanitize the model, presenting a major advantage over costly fine-tuning baselines.

Strong empirical results: Achieves state-of-the-art censorship rates on both OPEN-SORA and ZEROSCOPET2V across established benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench, SafeSora) while successfully preserving visual quality (FVD/FVMD) and prompt alignment (MM-Notox).

Rigorous evaluation and analysis: The paper includes thorough ablation studies regarding subspace rank, hyperparameter sensitivity, robustness to adversarial attacks, and an interesting study adapting image-unlearning baselines (UCE) to video.
weaknesses: Scaling limitations for multi-concept erasure: As shown in Appendix C.3 (Table 8), sequentially applying multiple refusal vectors (e.g., up to 5 concepts) leads to a significant increase in FVD (up to 579.37 on complex categories like Sequential Action Risk), indicating a degradation in visual quality when scaling to many concepts simultaneously.

Empirically-driven layer selection: The choice of injecting the update into specific layers (layers 17-18) is determined empirically. It is not fully clear if this specific location choice generalizes easily to other video models without requiring manual hyperparameter exploration.

Dependence on linear representation assumptions: The closed-form update relies on projecting onto a linear low-rank subspace. A discussion on the method's limitations or failure modes when target concepts are represented in highly non-linear manifolds within the network would strengthen the paper.

strengths: First training-free, closed-form weight update framework for video unlearning, eliminating the need for expensive fine-tuning or inference-time filtering.
The integration of contrastive Principal Component Analysis (cPCA) and low-rank factorization successfully isolates target unsafe concepts while preventing collateral forgetting of safe concepts.
Comprehensive evaluation on two diverse video generation models (Open-Sora and ZeroscopeT2V) across two established safety benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench and SafeSora).
Strong experimental results, demonstrating significant reduction in unsafe generations while preserving video quality (measured by FVD/FVMD) and prompt alignment (measured by MM-Notox).
A detailed and thorough appendix providing clear derivations of the weight update, hyperparameter analyses, and comparison against adapted text-based unlearning (UCE).
weaknesses: There is a minor mathematical/dimensional inconsistency on Page 5: if the matrix of differences $R$ is defined as $R \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times N}$, the covariance matrix should be computed as $C_r = \bar{R} \bar{R}^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times H}$ instead of $C_r = \bar{R}^{\top} \bar{R}$ (which would be in $\mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$). This typo also repeats for $C_e = \bar{E}^{\top} \bar{E}$.

While the training-free closed-form update is highly efficient, it relies on a small set of manual prompt pairs ($N=5$) to define the refusal vector. It remains slightly unclear how sensitive the method is if the target concept has very complex or multi-faceted semantic definitions that cannot be easily captured in five pairs.

The evaluation, although strong, would benefit from testing on even more recent large-scale open-weights video models such as CogVideoX or HunyuanVideo, which use different architectures and text encoders (e.g., T5).

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely topic: permanent safety alignment and concept unlearning in text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models without retraining or inference-time filtering.

The proposed method is computationally efficient and requires no retraining. It computes a closed-form weight update derived from a low-rank refusal vector using only a small set of safe/unsafe prompt pairs (e.g., 5 pairs).

The integration of contrastive Principal Component Analysis (cPCA) is mathematically sound and elegantly derived (as shown in the detailed proofs in Appendix B) to project out unsafe features while minimizing collateral semantic damage.

The evaluation is thorough, leveraging standard safety benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench and SafeSora) and appropriate metrics (FVD, MM-Notox, FVMD) to evaluate safety, video quality, and temporal consistency.
weaknesses: The terminology used throughout the evaluation tables is highly confusing. The paper refers to the metric as 'Censorship ↓', but a lower score indicates fewer unsafe generations. In standard English, a successful censorship mechanism should have a high censorship rate. This metric should be renamed to 'Unsafe Generation Rate', 'Violation Rate', or 'Safety Failure Rate' to avoid confusion.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental. The concept of refusal vectors is borrowed from LLM mechanistic interpretability, and cPCA is an established statistical technique. The primary contribution lies in adapting and projecting these concepts onto the cross-attention FFN layers of video diffusion architectures.

The evaluation is performed on relatively older/smaller open-source models (Open-Sora and ZeroscopeT2V). Evaluating the framework on larger, more state-of-the-art open-weights video models (e.g., CogVideoX or HunyuanVideo) would significantly boost the significance of the results.

While the paper evaluates semantic preservation using MM-Notox and FVD on the same categories, it lacks a comprehensive utility evaluation (e.g., using a general T2V capability benchmark like VBench) on a wide range of safe, completely unrelated prompts to rigorously prove that general video generation capability is preserved.
